title: Portable fire extinguisher + emergency/exit lighting inspection route (OSFM Class A distributor)
subindustry: Portable extinguisher inspection, maintenance, recharge, hydro (subcontracted) and emergency lighting testing
product_service: Annual extinguisher inspection/tagging, 6-year maintenance, recharge, replacement unit sales, signage/cabinets, plus monthly/annual emergency & exit light testing and battery/fixture replacement; hydrostatic testing subcontracted to a PHMSA RIN holder initially.
target_customer: Small and mid-size commercial occupancies in Chicagoland: offices, retail strips, restaurants, light industrial/warehouses, auto shops, churches, multifamily common areas, property managers of 5-200 buildings.
purchase_motivation: Code/AHJ fire inspections and insurer requirements (NFPA 101 2015 adopted statewide; extinguisher servicing restricted to OSFM-licensed firms); fines/violations; tenant lease obligations.
spending_evidence: Licensing regime restricts extinguisher servicing to OSFM-licensed distributors [A, WS05-S001, WS05-S003]; Cintas Fire Protection Services revenue grew to $929.1M in FY2026 from $728.6M in FY2024 [A, WS05-S024]; APi describes inspections as statutorily/insurance mandated recurring revenue [A, WS05-S019]. Chicago DOB issued extinguisher-related violations at 489 distinct addresses and emergency-lighting violations at 357 addresses in Nov 2025-Nov 2026 (DOB only; CFD enforcement not captured) [A, WS05-S035]. City of Chicago awarded Johnson Controls a 2020-2025 fire extinguisher & suppression services contract of ~$1.48M [A, WS05-S036].
representative_operators: Cintas Fire Protection - 4 Illinois locations with 80 OSFM employee licenses [A, WS05-S014]
Fox Valley Fire & Safety - 34 employee licenses [A, WS05-S014]
Pye-Barker Fire & Safety (consolidator, ~246 US locations) - 11 IL employee licenses [A/C, WS05-S014, WS05-S020]
~46 Illinois-list locations with a single licensed employee (owner-operators) [A, WS05-S014]
revenue_mechanism: Per-unit annual inspection fee + service-call minimum; per-unit maintenance/recharge fees; product resale; emergency-light test fees; repair pull-through.
typical_transaction_value: Analyst estimate: $10-25 per extinguisher annual inspection, typical small account 4-20 units -> $100-500/yr inspection plus $50-400 replacements/maintenance; multi-site property manager accounts $2k-20k/yr [E]
direct_costs: Technician labor, vehicle/fuel, tags/parts/agent, subcontracted hydrotesting, replacement-unit COGS, insurance ($1M liability required).
contribution_profit_note: Analyst model: one dense-route tech at ~$150k-250k annual revenue and ~$65k-80k loaded labor + ~$15k vehicle leaves ~$50k-110k contribution per route before overhead [E].
working_capital_note: Mostly invoiced net-15/30 to businesses; small inventory of extinguishers/parts ($3k-10k); annual billing concentrated in renewal months; low receivables risk but slow-pay property managers.
sales_cycle: Days to weeks for small businesses (decision by owner/manager); 1-3 months for property managers; renewals are annual and often auto-scheduled.
repeat_purchase: recurring-contract - annual inspection mandated each year; monthly/annual emergency lighting tests; 6-year maintenance and 12-year hydro cycles create predictable pull-through
acquisition_channels: Door-to-door/walk-in canvassing of strip centers and industrial parks
Referrals from fire inspectors' violation follow-ups (no solicitation of officials)
Cross-sell from adjacent trades (hood cleaners, alarm companies)
Buying routes from retiring owner-operators later (not initial entry)
Public Chicago building-violation records (extinguisher/emergency-lighting citations) as a prospect list [A, WS05-S035]
customer_accessibility: Buyers are visible (every commercial occupancy), decision-makers reachable in person, annual renewal moment creates switching opportunity; but many accounts are tied to incumbents by habit and multi-service bundles.
supplier_accessibility: Assumed accessible: extinguishers/parts via fire-equipment wholesalers; hydrotesting can be subcontracted to a RIN holder as the OSFM form permits [A, WS05-S001]. Specific wholesaler terms not verified.
competitive_intensity: moderate-high - ~184 active distributor licenses statewide incl. ~75 Chicagoland locations; Cintas, JCI, Fox Valley and PE consolidators active; many 1-2 person shops [A, WS05-S014]
entry_strategy: Hyper-dense micro-territory (a few ZIP codes), owner-operated responsiveness, all-in-one annual compliance package (extinguishers + emergency lights + exit signs + documentation portal), transparent flat pricing vs. national firms' add-on fees; target accounts dissatisfied with national route reps.
licenses: OSFM Fire Equipment Distributor license Class A $900/3 yrs; employee license Class 1 $300/3 yrs requiring ICC or NAFED portable-extinguisher certification (NAFED exam $320, open-book, no experience prerequisite listed); $1M liability insurance; workers comp; PHMSA RIN or contract RIN holder for hydro; age 18+ [A, WS05-S001, WS05-S002, WS05-S003; B, WS05-S025]. Local business licenses as applicable.
regulatory_barriers: Low-moderate: licensing achievable in ~1-3 months; Act carries a scheduled repeal date of 1 Jan 2028 (renewal status unverified) [A, WS05-S003]; emergency lighting repairs beyond battery/lamp swaps may need electrical licensing in Chicago (unverified).
operational_risks: Route density takes years; technician quality/tagging fraud liability; seasonality; customer concentration in property managers.
financial_risks: Low capital at risk; main risk is slow ramp leaving founder underpaid for 12-24 months; price competition from bundled national providers.
geographic_constraints: Local route business; Chicagoland density favorable; each additional location needs a separate OSFM distributor license [A, WS05-S003].
founder_expertise: Pass NAFED/ICC FE exam; learn NFPA 10 practices, recharge equipment, DOT cylinder rules; field sales.
staffing: Founder as first tech/salesperson; hire first tech at ~150-250 accounts; office admin/scheduler at ~3 techs.
automation_potential: Route optimization, renewal scheduling, digital inspection reports/barcodes, prospect lists from public business data, automated invoicing; physical inspection stays human.
delegation_potential: High once SOPs exist - standard technician role with certifications obtainable in weeks.
scalability: Regional density play; ceiling expands by adding suppression, alarm (via licensed partner), sprinkler (via hired DCP) lines; strategic exit to PE consolidators plausible later.
expansion: Kitchen suppression (WS05-003), hood cleaning referral partnerships, fire alarm (WS05-006), sprinkler ITM (WS05-002), first-aid cabinets/AED service, safety training.
critical_assumptions: Chicagoland pricing of $10-25/unit and service-call minimums holds [E]
A new entrant can win ~300-800 accounts within 3 years via canvassing
Hydrotesting can be subcontracted economically
OSFM Act is renewed past its 2028 sunset
unanswered_questions: Actual Chicagoland per-unit pricing and minimum charges (no primary pricing found)
Chicago-specific extinguisher rules (Chicago Fire Prevention Code) and whether city requires additional registration
Wholesaler access/terms for a new distributor
Churn rates of small commercial extinguisher accounts
failure_modes: Never reaching route density - drive time eats margin
Competing on price with Cintas bundles
Founder stuck as only technician (hours cap)

title: Local jan-san (janitorial & sanitation) distributor for Chicago-area facilities
subindustry: Janitorial/sanitation paper, liners, chemicals, dispensers, equipment
product_service: Recurring supply of can liners, towel/tissue, hand soap, floor and restroom chemicals, dispensers, mops/carts and small floor machines, delivered on scheduled routes; optional dispenser conversion programs and chemical-dilution system installs.
target_customer: Building service contractors (BSCs), property managers of offices/industrial parks, private schools and churches, light-industrial plants, auto dealers, non-acute healthcare in Chicago metro; 1-100 sites each.
purchase_motivation: Consumables they cannot run out of; labor savings from dilution systems; one-stop consolidated delivery; slow/unreliable service from consolidated incumbents.
spending_evidence: Paper & paper products merchant wholesalers (incl. jan-san paper) generated ~$103B sales at 23.9% gross margin in 2022 [C, WS16-S018]; consolidators Bunzl (GBP 11.8bn revenue) and Imperial Dade (230+ locations) are built on this spend [A/B, WS16-S030, WS16-S032].
representative_operators: Imperial Dade / BradyIFS (imperialbrady.com) — 13k+ associates, 230+ locations [B, WS16-S032]
Bunzl plc — 220-230+ acquisitions since 2004, operating margin 7.7% [A, WS16-S030, WS16-S031]
Essendant — two-step wholesaler supplying small jan-san resellers, Lincolnshire IL [B, WS16-S029]
revenue_mechanism: Buy-resell markup on consumables; equipment sales; occasional service/repair of floor machines.
typical_transaction_value: $300-$3,000 per delivery; small BSC accounts $10k-$60k/yr; multi-site accounts $100k+/yr [E]
direct_costs: Product COGS, delivery (van/driver or LTL), freight-in, rebates net of buying-group fees, dispenser placement capex.
contribution_profit_note: Incumbent industry implied pre-tax operating margin ~6% for paper/packaging wholesalers (GM 23.9% minus opex ~17.7%) [C, WS16-S019]; new entrant lacks rebates/volume pricing so expect 4-6 pts lower GM at start [E].
working_capital_note: Net-30 receivables from commercial accounts (BSCs often pay slow); starter inventory $10-40k unless drop-shipping via two-step wholesaler; supplier credit after credit application (Essendant can approve in days) [B, WS16-S028]; dispenser programs tie up capital until recouped.
sales_cycle: 2-8 weeks for small accounts (trial order, price comparison); 3-6 months for multi-site BSCs/property managers.
repeat_purchase: consumable-replenishment — weekly/monthly reorders; dispenser placements lock in towel/soap refills
acquisition_channels: Door-to-door/field sales to BSCs and property managers
Cleaning contractor associations and local BSC networks
customer_accessibility: Buyers numerous and identifiable (BSCs, facility managers); purchasing is relationship + price driven; many accounts tied to consolidated distributors via contracts or dispenser placements.
supplier_accessibility: Assumed/partly confirmed: two-step wholesaler (Essendant) sells to resellers meeting volume minimum + resale certificate [B, WS16-S028]; buying groups (AFFLINK etc.) admit independent distributors but criteria not published but publish no criteria or fees [B, WS16-S042]; brand-level authorization varies (e.g., Rubbermaid online reseller controls) [B, WS16-S033].
competitive_intensity: high — national consolidators, Amazon Business, Staples/ODP, Grainger, plus entrenched local independents
entry_strategy: Service wedge in a dense geography: guaranteed next-day delivery, dispenser conversion + dilution-control installs, consolidated billing, and targeting BSCs underserved after consolidator acquisitions; plan exit/roll-up potential since consolidators acquire local houses.
licenses: Illinois business registration (Secretary of State LLC filing) and IDOR registration (Form REG-1) to collect ROT and issue resale certificates (CRT-61) [A, WS16-S036]; general liability/product liability insurance; no professional license; USDOT/hazmat awareness for transporting limited-quantity cleaning chemicals (MISSING detail)
regulatory_barriers: Low. SDS/GHS labeling compliance for chemicals; green-certified product requirements in some public contracts.
operational_risks: Delivery reliability, stockouts, driver turnover, dispenser loss, price wars on paper.
financial_risks: Thin margins; paper/resin price swings; customer concentration on a few BSCs; bad debt from small contractors.
geographic_constraints: Route density matters: Chicago metro first; each new metro needs a branch or 3PL.
founder_expertise: Product knowledge (chemistry dilution, paper specs), pricing, purchasing, route logistics; ISSA-type training.
staffing: Year 1: founder + part-time driver; Year 2: inside CSR/purchasing, 1-2 outside reps; warehouse lead by $1.5M revenue.
automation_potential: AI-assisted quoting and order entry, reorder prediction per account, route optimization, invoice/AR follow-up; delivery and field selling stay human.
delegation_potential: Good — distribution roles (driver, CSR, buyer, outside rep) have an established labor market.
scalability: Moderate: branch replication and tuck-ins; consolidators prove scale but at ~7-8% operating margin [A, WS16-S030].
expansion: Floor-machine dealership/service (WS16-020), foodservice disposables (WS16-002), PPE (WS16-004), facility packaging (WS16-003); sell to a consolidator.
roic_note: At ~$2M revenue: receivables ~$165k + inventory ~$120k + van/dispensers ~$40k less payables ~$100k ≈ $225k invested for ~$80-120k operating profit ≈ 35-55% [E]; drop-ship start improves early ROIC.
critical_assumptions: A newcomer can buy at competitive cost via two-step wholesaler/buying group within 6-12 months
Service wedge wins BSC accounts despite consolidator pricing
Route density reachable within ~20-mile radius
unanswered_questions: Buying-group (AFFLINK, Network Services) admission criteria and fees
Essendant minimum annual purchase volume and drop-ship fees
Number of independent jan-san distributors in Chicago metro (CBP NAICS 423850 by county)
Typical jan-san small-distributor gross margin (ISSA benchmarks inaccessible — 403)
failure_modes: Price-only competition against consolidators erodes GM below 20%
Too few accounts per route; delivery cost swamps margin
Over-stocking inventory and slow-paying BSCs drain cash
Key account acquired by a national BSC that switches to national contract

title: Outsourced quantity takeoff & estimating for specialty subcontractors (remote, AI-assisted)
product_service: Per-bid quantity takeoffs and priced estimates (drywall, paint, flooring, concrete, roofing, electrical device counts) from bid PDFs, delivered in 24-72 hours; monthly retainer for a set bid volume.
target_customer: Owners/estimators of specialty subcontractors with ~$1-20M revenue that bid many jobs and lack estimating staff.
purchase_motivation: Subs win a small share of bids, so estimating labor per win is high; owners are the bottleneck; faster turnaround lets them bid more.
spending_evidence: Large fragmented buyer base: 515,720 US specialty-trade employer establishments averaging $2.49M receipts; Illinois 18,900 [C, WS10-S022]. Direct evidence of outsourced-estimating spend and prices MISSING (search budget exhausted before pricing research).
representative_operators: Remote/offshore estimating services and AI takeoff software vendors exist; names, sizes and prices not verified in this session [E]
revenue_mechanism: Per takeoff fee by sheet count/trade, or monthly subscription for N takeoffs.
typical_transaction_value: Hypothesis $200-$800 per trade takeoff or $1,500-$5,000/month retainer [E].
direct_costs: Estimator labor (US or offshore), takeoff software licences, AI/API costs, QA review.
contribution_profit_note: A $400 takeoff needing ~3 estimator-hours at $25-40/hr loaded leaves ~$280-$325 [E].
working_capital_note: Retainers billable in advance; per-job fees paid on delivery by card/ACH; negligible inventory.
sales_cycle: Short (days-weeks) once trust is established via a free/sample takeoff.
acquisition_channels: Public bid lists and plan-holder lists (named subs bidding public work)
Supplier partnerships (distributors offer takeoff to contractor customers)
customer_accessibility: Many buyers with frequent need, identifiable via public bid documents; trust in accuracy is the hurdle.
supplier_accessibility: Estimator labor available remotely (assumed); software tools commercially available (assumed).
competitive_intensity: high: offshore estimating shops and self-serve AI takeoff software compete on price [E]
entry_strategy: Pick 1-2 trades, guarantee turnaround and accuracy (credit for errors), publish trade-specific assemblies; sell to subs in a few metros, then nationally.
licenses: No licence for takeoff/estimating (not engineering); general business registration; E&O insurance prudent [E].
regulatory_barriers: Minimal; liability for estimating errors is contractual.
operational_risks: Accuracy errors lose bids or cause money-losing wins; turnaround spikes at bid deadlines; scope-reading skill is scarce.
financial_risks: Low capital; main risk is error liability and churn.
geographic_constraints: None; remote delivery nationally; local pricing data needed for priced estimates.
founder_expertise: Blueprint reading, trade scopes, assemblies and unit pricing for chosen trades; QA processes.
staffing: Founder + 1-3 trained estimators by year 2; QA lead.
automation_potential: High: AI-assisted area/count extraction from PDFs, spec parsing, assembly mapping. Human: scope interpretation, exclusions, QA, pricing judgment. Risk: the same AI lets subs self-serve, eroding the service.
delegation_potential: Good: estimator role is standard and trainable; QA can be delegated.
scalability: National market; scales with estimators; commoditization pressure limits margin.
expansion: Bid-management outsourcing, submittal prep (WS10-003), supplier-sponsored takeoff programs, estimating for GCs.
roic_note: Asset-light; <$10k capital; ROIC very high if demand exists [E].
critical_assumptions: Subs will pay $200-$800 per takeoff or retainers [E]
AI tools cut takeoff hours enough to beat offshore pricing
Accuracy can be maintained without trade experience
unanswered_questions: Market prices of outsourced takeoffs by trade
Share of subs that already outsource or use AI takeoff software

Chicago CDPH inspected 10,605 distinct food licenses in Nov 2025-Nov 2026, indicating the size of the city's food-establishment base [A, WS05-S034].
representative_operators: Cintas, Fox Valley, JCI and Pye-Barker hold both A and B classes [A, WS05-S014]
Many small A,B distributors on OSFM list [A, WS05-S014]

regulatory_barriers: Low-moderate; manufacturer authorization is the practical gate.
operational_risks: Liability if system fails in a fire; restaurant churn.

Restaurants switch providers on service quality

title: Industrial & warehouse packaging distributor (stretch film, corrugated, tape, equipment service) for Chicago logistics/manufacturing

representative_operators: Uline (catalog direct; private, figures not sourced)
Imperial Dade / BradyIFS industrial packaging [B, WS16-S032]
revenue_mechanism: Markup on consumables; equipment sales/rental; service calls; custom box margin.
typical_transaction_value: $1,000-$10,000 per monthly order for a mid-size warehouse; equipment $8k-$40k [E]

staffing: Founder + driver; equipment tech by year 2; inside CSR.
automation_potential: Spec comparison, quote generation, reorder forecasting from usage; equipment service is human.
delegation_potential: Good — standard distribution and technician roles.
scalability: Moderate: replicate in other logistics hubs; add custom corrugated brokerage.
expansion: Jan-san for same facilities (WS16-001), AIDC labels (WS16-011), racking (WS16-018), safety (WS16-004).

Supplier pricing for a new distributor allows ≥20% GM

Manufacturer minimums for direct accounts (film, tape)
Chicago-area count of independent packaging distributors

title: Lien-rights & payment-compliance administration for Illinois subcontractors and suppliers
product_service: Tracking Illinois notice deadlines per job, preparing preliminary notices, collecting sworn statements and lien waivers, deadline alerts and payment follow-up; lien recording handled through a partner attorney.
target_customer: Small/mid subs and material suppliers (lumber yards, electrical/plumbing distributors) selling on credit to contractors.
purchase_motivation: Non-payment risk under pay-when-paid; Illinois sub notice windows (90 days after last work; 60 days from start on owner-occupied single-family) and 4-month recording deadline [C, WS10-S030]; retainage withholding [A, WS10-S029].
spending_evidence: National lien-rights software/services exist (Levelset; ownership/terms not verified) [E]; Illinois-specific spend MISSING.
representative_operators: Levelset (construction payment/lien software; cited for Illinois deadlines) [C, WS10-S030]
revenue_mechanism: Per-notice fee or monthly subscription by job volume; referral of lien filings to attorneys (fee splitting with non-lawyers is restricted - must be structured carefully).
typical_transaction_value: Hypothesis $30-$100 per notice; $300-$1,500/month per active supplier [E].
direct_costs: Admin labor, certified mail/postage, software.
contribution_profit_note: High per-notice margin; volume-dependent [E].
working_capital_note: Subscription billed monthly in advance; negligible inventory.
sales_cycle: 1-2 months; credit managers at suppliers are the natural buyers.
customer_accessibility: Suppliers identifiable; established software competitors already sell to them.
supplier_accessibility: Requires an attorney partner for lien recording and legal advice.
competitive_intensity: high: national software platforms and law firms [E]
entry_strategy: Illinois-only depth (Chicago + Cook County recording specifics), done-for-you service rather than software.
licenses: No specific licence for administrative tracking; preparing/recording lien claims for others may constitute unauthorized practice of law in Illinois - legal review required [E].
regulatory_barriers: Unauthorized-practice-of-law boundary; rules on lawyer fee-sharing.
operational_risks: A missed deadline destroys a client's lien rights (high liability).
geographic_constraints: Illinois law-specific; expansion needs state-by-state rules.
founder_expertise: Illinois Mechanics Lien Act, Prompt Payment Act, credit management.
automation_potential: AI/software: deadline computation, document generation, waiver tracking; human: legal judgment, disputes.
scalability: Regional; software-like recurring revenue but crowded.
expansion: Collections (WS02 cross-stream), credit reports on contractors, closeout support.
critical_assumptions: A compliant structure exists that avoids UPL
Suppliers prefer done-for-you service over software
unanswered_questions: Illinois rules on non-lawyers preparing lien notices vs lien claims

title: Backflow prevention assembly testing & repair route (CCCDI) with hired licensed plumbers

spending_evidence: Annual testing mandate in 35 IAC 604/653 and 77 IAC 890.1130 [A, WS05-S006, WS05-S008]; Pye-Barker lists backflow among services [C, WS05-S020].
representative_operators: Plumbing contractors and fire sprinkler firms (not enumerated)
revenue_mechanism: Per-device test fee + filing; repair parts and labor.
typical_transaction_value: Analyst estimate: $75-200 per device test; repair/rebuild $150-800 [E]
direct_costs: Licensed plumber-CCCDI labor, test kit calibration, vehicle, repair parts, utility filing fees.

working_capital_note: Net-30 commercial; payroll for licensed tester precedes route density.
sales_cycle: Short - compliance notices drive inbound demand around due dates.
acquisition_channels: Owners responding to utility notices (SEO, tester listings)
customer_accessibility: High - mandated annually, buyers search for testers; but price-driven.

financial_risks: Licensed labor cost compresses margin on $75-200 tickets.
automation_potential: Due-date prediction from utility notices, booking, automated filing; testing stays human.
expansion: Fire sprinkler ITM, plumbing repair, grease interceptor service.
roic_note: Moderate capital; returns limited by licensed labor cost [E].
critical_assumptions: Can hire CCCDI-plumbers at margin-viable wage
unanswered_questions: Chicago DWM backflow program details/filing fees

title: Lab supplies distributor for biotech startups and academic labs (Chicago/Illinois)
product_service: Pipette tips, tubes, plates, gloves, chemicals/reagents (non-controlled), small benchtop equipment; same-day local delivery; private-label equivalents.
target_customer: Lab managers/PIs at biotech startups (Fulton Market, incubators), university labs, hospital research labs, contract labs.
